desc:
A grid matrix contains only 0 and 1. Among all rectangles (blocks of consecutive rows and columns) whose cells are all 1, find the one with the largest perimeter. A rectangle covering h rows and w columns has perimeter 2 * (h + w).

Return that largest perimeter, or 0 if the grid contains no 1.

Example: [[1,1,1,1],[0,1,0,0]] has the 1 by 4 strip of ones, perimeter 10; the best other choice is smaller. A grid with a single 1 returns 4.
constraints: All rows have the same length
hints: Area-based answers do not apply here, but notice that enlarging a rectangle never decreases its perimeter. So only rectangles that cannot be enlarged matter.
For each row as the bottom edge, let h[c] be the number of consecutive ones ending at that row in column c. A rectangle that cannot be enlarged has height equal to the smallest h in its column range.
Run the histogram stack on each row. Whenever a bar of height hh > 0 is popped with block width w, evaluate 2 * (hh + w) and keep the maximum.
editorial: Any all-ones rectangle can be grown until it is maximal (it cannot grow up, down, left or right), and growing never reduces the perimeter, so an optimal rectangle can be assumed maximal. A maximal rectangle with bottom row r has a height equal to the minimum of h[c] over its columns, where h are the run heights ending at row r, and its columns form the widest block in which all h[c] are at least that minimum.

That is exactly what the histogram stack produces: when a bar is popped, its height is the minimum of the block and the block's width is determined by the new stack top and the current index. Evaluate the perimeter 2 * (height + width) for every pop with positive height, for every row, and return the maximum. Note that a wide, flat block can beat a tall, narrow one with a larger area, which is why we cannot just reuse the maximal-area answer. Time O(R * C), space O(C).
